header:
Date: 2027-11-27
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Rios (Redwood), Alex Moreno (Cobalt CTO), Priya Shah (Cobalt ML Eng), Marcus Lee (Cobalt SRE), Nora Chen (Cobalt PM)
summary: Discovery focused on model selection for Cobalt's multi-lingual customer support agent. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs, context length (8k vs 32k+), tool-calling support, multilingual quality, latency/cost targets, security (SOC 2, SSO/SAML, KMS), and next steps to run a pilot with representative prompts.
topics: Multilingual performance and fine-tuning vs prompt engineering
Tool-calling / function calling support and safety
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs
Latency and cost targets, autoscaling and batching
Security/compliance: SOC2, SAML, KMS, audit logs
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, I'll hand it over to Samira in a sec to do a quick tech intro.
[00:08] Alex: Hey thanks, appreciate it. we got the calendar, excited to talk through model selection.
[00:12] Samira: Cool, hi all, I'm Samira, Redwood SE. quick agenda: understand current infra, key requirements — context length, multilingual, tool calls — and then map to hosted/dedicated/private options and model options.
[00:25] Priya: Quick heads up — our main use case is customer support automation for EMEA + APAC, so english + french + japanese mainly, and we sometimes need very long context for transcript summarization (20k tokens plus) so context is a big one.
[00:40] Marcus: And from infra side we need low tail latency for live chat, target p95 < 300ms for short requests (1-2 turns), offline batch summarization can be higher.
[00:54] Nora: Security's also important — SOC2 required, SSO via SAML, and we'd like KMS integration for keys, plus audit logs retention.
[01:06] Jordan: Great, those are the main things we see with other customers. Samira, model options?
[01:11] Samira: Sure. For open models we typically compare Mistral and Llama-family variants, Harmony-style 8k vs 32k context models. Redwood also offers curated runs of larger context open models and quantized variants for cost. For commercial models, teams compare Anthropic/claude and OpenAI, but you lose some deployment flex, and costs can differ.
[01:28] Alex: For us open models are preferable for deployment flexibility but we need tool-calling — do these open models support function-calling reliably?
[01:36] Samira: Good question. Function-calling is largely an application-layer pattern. Many open models can do structured outputs; some of our runtime work adds a small adapter for consistent tool-calls and schema enforcement. There can be hallucination risks and we add guard rails.
[01:50] Priya: When you say adapters, is that part of hosted or do we need dedicated/private? we want to keep vector DB calls and internal APIs private.
[01:59] Diego: The adapter lives in the Redwood runtime; in hosted we do callouts from our infra but we can configure private connectors or enable VPC egress in Dedicated/Private. For sensitive internal APIs customers usually prefer Dedicated or Private to avoid routing through shared network paths — that's a policy decision for you.
[02:18] Alex: How about context length — we said 20k tokens. are there reliable 32k open models?
[02:24] Samira: Yes, there are 32k-context variants in the Mistral and Llama-X families and some specialized long-context open models. Performance and cost tradeoffs: longer context usually increases memory footprint and latency per request. For summarization batch jobs you can use chunking + KV cache to stitch together. Redwood supports KV cache and prefix caching to reduce cost for repeated contexts.
[02:48] Marcus: You mentioned KV cache — are you doing persistent KV cache across requests? we have frequent follow-ups for same customer session.
[02:55] Samira: We support session-level KV caching; it's configurable. small note — sometimes our transcriber exports show K V cash spelled weird in logs, lol. but functionally it's persistent session cache for compatible models.
[03:08] Priya: Multilingual — we need high quality in Japanese and French. do you have evals or benchmarks for that?
[03:16] Samira: We have per-language evals. open models differ: some Llama-like models do decently, Mistral variants are strong on european languages, and a few Asia-focused models do better on Japanese. We recommend running a small eval with your real prompts — that gives the most signal.
[03:31] Alex: latency — for live chat we need <300ms p95 for short prompts. is that feasible with hosted?
[03:36] Diego: Hosted can achieve low latency for short requests using optimized runtimes and warm KV caches; but to guarantee tail latency at scale teams often pick Dedicated with reserved GPU pools to avoid noisy neighbor effects. We also offer burst capacity.
[03:50] Marcus: Cost — rough order of magnitude difference between hosted and dedicated?
[03:53] Jordan: Hosted is usage-based and simpler, good for early pilots. Dedicated is reserved capacity so you get better predictable throughput per cost but need a commit. Private adds platform fee for on-prem. We'll send a pricing sheet.
[04:05] Priya: We're also considering quantized models to lower cost — how good is quantization for multilingual and long-context?
[04:12] Samira: 8-bit and 4-bit quantization work well for many LLMs; however, some languages or specialized tokens can degrade slightly. For long-context, quantization interacts with memory and kernel selection; our runtime recommends model+quantization pairs per workload. We'll include recommended profiles in the spreadsheet.
[04:31] Nora: Security again — if we go private, can we bring our own key manager (HSM/KMS)?
[04:36] Diego: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. Dedicated supports KMS federation and audit logs; hosted supports envelope encryption with Redwood-managed KMS but we can discuss BYOK for enterprise contracts.
[04:50] Alex: Any customers doing hybrid — hosted for non-sensitive, private for PII workloads?
[04:54] Jordan: Yes, hybrid routing is common — route by policy (tenant, region, sensitivity). Redwood can fallback to cheaper recents or alternate models when capacity constrained.
[05:05] Priya: Tool-calling safety — we talked about schema enforcement but how do you prevent unauthorized calls?
[05:12] Samira: We provide RBAC and route-level policies. tool calls are proxied through the runtime where we can add allowlists, rate limits, and sanitization. Audit logs show call-level metadata.
[05:25] Marcus: Network — if we go VPC and Private control plane, how does network egress look for integrations with our DB in VPC?
[05:34] Diego: Private can be fully air-gapped or VPC-peered; Dedicated offers VPC egress and private endpoints. We'll capture network config during the technical deep-dive.
[05:45] Alex: For the pilot, what would you need from us?
[05:49] Samira: Representative prompt set, traffic profile (qps, concurrency), example documents for summarization, target languages, and a success metric (latency/cost/accuracy). We'll run a 2-4 week pilot with 1-2 model variants and compare results.
[06:05] Priya: On accuracy, we'd also want an eval on hallucination and tool-call correctness.
[06:09] Samira: Absolutely — we tie quality monitoring to prompt sets and can alert on regressions.
[06:14] Alex: A couple of nitty gritty questions: does Redwood runtime support function calling across model families consistently? sometimes we see JSON output formatting differences.
[06:23] Samira: Correct, different models produce different structured outputs. Redwood runtime's adapter normalizes shapes and enforces JSON schema; we also have a heuristics layer for common parsing errors. It reduces brittle integration.
[06:34] Nora: Do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO reports available for review?
[06:38] Jordan: Yes we do — we'll share SOC2 docs and our security pack. For enterprise contracts we can include additional audit clauses.
[06:45] Marcus: Regarding concurrency — our peak concurrent chat sessions could be ~600 sessions. what's the right capacity?
[06:52] Diego: Depends on request QPS per session and tokens per request. For short chat turns, you can scale horizontally with more instances and batching. Dedicated reserved pool would be sized based on your qps baseline; we'll work with your ops team.
[07:08] Alex: Any limitations on model tokenizers causing tokenization differences across languages? we've seen odd token counts for japanese.
[07:16] Samira: Yes, tokenization can vary; we recommend measuring tokens per message with candidate models. sometimes you need subword tokenization changes to optimize.
[07:27] Priya: What about compliance for EU data residency?
[07:30] Jordan: We have region-specific hosting and can pin data to EU regions on Dedicated/Private. We'll document region options in the follow-ups.
[07:41] Alex: About the pilot models — would you recommend starting with an 8k model for chat and a 32k for summarization?
[07:48] Samira: That's a common approach: 8k or 16k for interactive chat to keep latency low, 32k+ for summarization offline. If you need unified model for both, we can test 32k variants but expect higher latency and cost.
[08:02] Nora: Licensing concerns — open models vs managed commercial models. licensing for fine-tuning?
[08:09] Jordan: Open models generally allow fine-tuning but check individual model licenses. Redwood can help with model management and versioning. Commercial models have usage terms and different privacy guarantees.
[08:22] Marcus: Can you run A/B for us during the pilot to compare model variants?
[08:26] Samira: Yes we support canary and A/B rollouts with metrics collection. we can instrument latency, cost, and custom quality metrics tied to prompts.
[08:36] Alex: For the tool-calling gate — do you have a way to test malicious or unexpected tool inputs?
[08:42] Diego: We do safety fuzz tests and schema validation; runtime also supports allowlist and sandboxing for external calls.
[08:50] Priya: We'll want to measure token-level cost — does Redwood show per-token breakdown?
[08:55] Jordan: Yes Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route dashboards, and traces.
[09:03] Alex: Any experience with Japanese-specific models?
[09:06] Samira: A handful of open models focused on Asian languages show stronger performance; we'll include candidates. But empirical eval on your prompts is the right signal.
[09:16] Priya: For long transcripts, do you recommend retrieval-augmented pipelines or extended context?
[09:22] Samira: For 100k+ docs retrieval + RAG with chunking is typical. Extended context models are newer but can be expensive; hybrid approach often best.
[09:33] Marcus: How soon could we get a cost estimate for Dedicated pool for our expected load?
[09:37] Jordan: We'll size it after we get your qps and tokens-per-request. Jordan to follow up with a sizing worksheet.
[09:46] Alex: Are there any gotchas with model quantization for Japanese tokens?
[09:51] Samira: Slight degradation sometimes; we'll run quantized vs FP16 comparisons in the benchmark.
[09:58] Nora: Ok let's talk timeline: we want a pilot in Q1 — is that realistic?
[10:02] Jordan: Yes Q1 pilot is doable. We'll start pilot scoping now.
[10:07] Priya: One last question — does Redwood support tool chaining (call tool A then B) and guaranteed ordering?
[10:12] Diego: The runtime can orchestrate chains and maintain deterministic ordering if you use the runtime's tool abstraction; for ad-hoc models you might need additional orchestration.
[10:21] Samira: I'll note to include an example of the adapter config for tool chaining.
[10:25] Alex: Great, that helps. can you also share a sample contract term for data retention?
[10:30] Jordan: Yes will include in the security pack.
[10:34] Nora: Thanks everyone.
[10:36] Jordan: Recap: we'll send pricing, benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2/security pack, and schedule SE deep-dive. Customer will share prompts and traffic profile. Action items as discussed.
[10:47] Alex: Thanks, talk soon.
[10:49] End of call
